# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** Associate
**Date:** November 24, 2026
**Re:** Dribas Brewing Company, LLC / Brikon Systems, Inc.: Review of the BrewLedger License Documents, Issues and Recommended Fixes

**Privileged & Confidential: Attorney Work Product**

---

## 1. Summary

I reviewed all seven documents in the folder:

- the Software License Agreement dated January 15, 2026 (the "**SLA**");
- the Side Letter of the same date;
- the Data Processing Addendum of the same date (the "**DPA**");
- Amendment No. 1 dated September 15, 2026 (the "**Amendment**");
- the December 8, 2025 Term Sheet;
- Brikon's superseded December 19, 2025 draft; and
- Dribas's January 12, 2026 board consent.

Many of the issues below turn on one structural point. **Under SLA Section 15.6 (Order of Precedence), signed amendments and side letters prevail first, then the DPA, then the SLA.** So the DPA prevails over the SLA in any conflict, and the Amendment prevails over both.

Bottom line for the client:

1. **Dribas probably did not validly terminate.** The Side Letter window closed July 30, 2026, and the August Notice went out August 14, 2026. The stated termination date of November 12, 2026 has now passed. Dribas should keep performing and must not act as though the SLA has ended.
2. **The Amendment inverted the liability-cap carve-out.** Brikon's IP indemnity is now capped. Dribas's new regulatory/data indemnity to Brikon is uncapped.
3. **The DPA quietly narrows "Customer Data" to Personal Data.** Through the precedence clause, this arguably strips the SLA's anti-use and anti-training protection from Dribas's recipes, formulations and production data.
4. **The exclusivity covenant is far broader than the deal.** It covers worldwide brewery management, inventory, POS and distribution software, and it binds Affiliates. The Term Sheet scope was production-scheduling software at Wilmington and Dover only. Dribas may already be in breach through its taproom POS.
5. **The DPA moves data disputes to New York law and New York County courts.** This splits any data incident away from the SLA's Delaware/New Castle County forum.

All five points give Dribas reasons to seek a single **Amendment No. 2**. Brikon has missed the Brewhouse Integration Module (BIM) Acceptance Deadline and the Module is still in remediation. That gives Dribas meaningful leverage to negotiate the fixes below in exchange for resolving the August Notice dispute.

---

## 2. Issues in Priority Order

### Priority 1 (Most Urgent): The Side Letter Termination Window Expired Before the August Notice

**Where:**
- Side Letter Section 2.2 (Termination Right), read with Section 2.1 (Acceptance Deadline of June 30, 2026).
- Amendment Recitals B and C and Section 6 (Reservation of Rights).

**What the documents say:**
- **Acceptance Deadline.** Side Letter Section 2.1 required the BIM to be Accepted at both Sites by June 30, 2026.
- **Termination Right.** If it was not, Section 2.2 lets Dribas terminate the entire SLA with no fee. The Termination Notice must be "delivered no later than thirty (30) days after the Acceptance Deadline", which is **July 30, 2026**.
- **The missed deadline.** Amendment Recital B confirms the BIM was not Accepted at either Site by the Acceptance Deadline. The trigger was therefore met.
- **The August Notice.** Amendment Recital C records that Dribas delivered the notice on **August 14, 2026**, which is fifteen days after the window closed. It stated a termination date of November 12, 2026.
- **Positions.** Brikon disputed the notice by letter dated August 28, 2026. Dribas maintains the notice is effective. Section 6 of the Amendment reserves both sides' rights and requires continued performance under SLA Section 14.3.

**Why it matters:**
- **The notice is likely ineffective.** On the face of the documents it is untimely. Nothing in the Side Letter extends the window:
  - Section 6.3 says Brikon's delay notices (or its failure to give them) do not affect the Acceptance Deadline or the Termination Right.
  - Section 2.3 dispenses with cure and escalation, but says nothing about the 30-day exercise period.
  - SLA Section 15.8 says Brikon's failure to object promptly is not a waiver.
- **Treating the SLA as ended would be dangerous.** Today is November 24, 2026, past the stated November 12 effective date. If Dribas stops paying, stops cooperating or migrates off the platform, it risks committing a material breach under SLA Section 12.2. That would hand Brikon a termination-for-cause claim. It could also forfeit the refund and transition protections Dribas would want. For example, SLA Section 12.5 transition assistance is withheld where Brikon terminates for Dribas's non-payment.
- **The reservation protects positions, not results.** Amendment Section 6.2 means Dribas has not waived its position by signing the Amendment or continuing to pay. It does not cure the lateness.
- **Board governance.** Board Consent Section 9.3(a) requires prior Board approval for a termination notice, or the CEO emergency procedure with consultation. We should confirm the August Notice was properly authorized. That will not fix timeliness, but Brikon may raise it.

**Recommended fix / next steps:**
1. **Advise the client not to treat the SLA as terminated.** Dribas should keep paying undisputed Fees, using a written reservation of rights. It should keep the legacy systems running in parallel as permitted by Side Letter Section 4.6 and Amendment Section 5.6, and it should not decommission anything.
2. **Do not litigate the August Notice as the lead position.** It is weak. Use it instead as a bargaining chip toward a negotiated exit or a negotiated waiver. The best outcome is that Brikon agrees in Amendment No. 2 to treat the Termination Right as timely exercised, or grants a fresh, dated termination window tied to the BIM Remediation Plan.
3. **Develop alternative termination grounds.**
   - *SLA Section 4.4(c).* If the BIM fails the Acceptance Criteria after the second retest, Dribas may terminate as to that Module with a refund of all Fees paid for it. We should track the retest dates under the BIM Remediation Plan (Amendment Section 5.1(d)).
   - *SLA Section 12.2.* Brikon's failure to meet its Side Letter Section 2.1 covenant ("Licensor shall complete … no later than June 30, 2026") is arguably a material breach. Section 2.3 excludes cure only for the Termination Right, so a Section 12.2 notice with a 30-day cure period should be considered. It must follow SLA Section 14.1 escalation, which Amendment Section 6.4 expressly allows.
   - *SLA Section 5.5.* Chronic availability failure, if the service-level history supports it.
   - *Non-renewal.* Calendar the non-renewal deadline under SLA Section 12.1. The Initial Term ends January 15, 2029, so notice is due by mid-October 2028.
4. **Gather the facts:** the actual delivery method and date of the August Notice under SLA Section 15.5, all Brikon delay notices under Side Letter Section 6.3, and Board authorization.

---

### Priority 2 (High): The Amendment Shifted the Liability-Cap Carve-Out, So Brikon's IP Indemnity Is Now Capped and Dribas's New Indemnity Is Uncapped

**Where:**
- Amendment Section 3, which deletes and replaces SLA Section 10 in its entirety.
- SLA Section 11.3(a), which was not conformed.

**What the documents say:**
- **Original structure.** SLA Section 11.3(a) excludes "a party's obligations under Section 10.1" from both the consequential-damages exclusion (Section 11.1) and the cap (Section 11.2). In the original SLA, Section 10.1 was Brikon's IP infringement indemnity. This matches Term Sheet Section 11.3(a), which uncaps "Brikon's IP infringement indemnity", and Brikon's own December draft.
- **Restated Section 10.** Amendment Section 3 renumbers the provisions:
  - New **Section 10.1** is a **Licensee Indemnity**. Dribas must defend, indemnify and hold harmless Brikon against third-party *and regulatory* claims arising from labels, formulas, Regulatory Submission Data, regulatory filings and alcohol-law compliance. The coverage includes fines and penalties.
  - Brikon's IP indemnity moves to new **Section 10.2**.
- **No conforming change.** The Amendment does not change Section 11.3(a). It prevails under SLA Section 15.6. Amendment Section 1.3 freezes section references *within the Amendment*, but it does not rewrite the SLA's own cross-reference.

**Why it matters:**
- **Brikon's IP indemnity is now capped.** It falls within the Section 11.2 cap of fees paid or payable in the prior 12 months, currently about $96,000 (plus $18,000 once the LFC Module is invoiced), and within the Section 11.1 consequential-damages exclusion. A third-party infringement suit over a platform that runs Dribas's production could easily exceed that.
- **Section 11.3(e) does not fill the gap.** It covers a Party's infringement of *the other Party's* IP, not third-party claims.
- **Dribas's new indemnity is uncapped.** It is also outside the consequential-damages exclusion, and it covers regulatory fines and penalties. That is open-ended exposure in a heavily regulated industry, beginning as the LFC Module goes live.
- **The flip is hard to spot.** Each provision reads as ordinary drafting on its own. SLA Section 15.16 bars contra proferentem. Dribas's best argument is mutual intent based on the Term Sheet. The SLA's integration clause (Section 15.7) makes that argument uphill, so we should not rely on it.

**Recommended fix:**
- In Amendment No. 2, amend SLA Section 11.3(a) to read "**Licensor's obligations under Section 10.2**". This restores the agreed position.
- Expressly confirm that Dribas's Section 10.1 indemnity is **subject to** Sections 11.1 and 11.2. Alternatively, give it a separate, modest sub-cap, and exclude regulatory fines that Brikon's own Errors contribute to. The existing carve-backs in new Section 10.3 help here.
- Until fixed, advise the client to be cautious about expanding LFC Module use, and to review its own insurance coverage for regulatory and labeling claims (see Board Consent Section 8.5).

---

### Priority 3 (High): The DPA's Narrow "Customer Data" Definition Overrides the SLA and Exposes Recipes and Production Data

**Where:**
- DPA Section 1.1.
- SLA Sections 1.4 and 7.3, read with SLA Section 15.6.

**What the documents say:**
- **SLA definition.** SLA Section 1.4 defines "Customer Data" broadly to mean "all data Licensee submits, including recipes, formulations, production records and distributor sales data", plus outputs and derivatives.
- **SLA use restriction.** SLA Section 7.3 bars Brikon from using Customer Data except to serve Dribas. In particular, Brikon may not use it to "develop, train, benchmark or improve products or services for any other person."
- **DPA definition.** DPA Section 1.1 defines the same capitalized term as only "**Personal Data that Licensor Processes on behalf of Licensee**". The definition is not limited to "this Addendum."
- **Precedence.** The DPA prevails over the SLA in a conflict under SLA Section 15.6, so the narrow definition arguably controls everywhere the term appears.

**Why it matters:**
- **The core data protections may shrink to personal data only.** If the DPA definition controls, SLA Section 7.3 protects only personal data. The same applies to the other Customer-Data-based protections: ownership (7.1), security (7.4), incident notice (7.5) and return and deletion (7.8).
- **Recipes and production data would fall outside the anti-training bar.** Dribas's recipes, formulations, production records and distributor sales data are what the Board describes as among its "most valuable trade secrets" (Board Consent Section 8.2). Under this reading, Brikon could argue it may use them to train or benchmark across its other brewery customers.
- **The fallback is weaker.** SLA Section 8 confidentiality still treats trade secrets, including recipes and formulations, as protected, which gives some protection. But Section 8 defines Confidential Information to "include Customer Data." It is less explicit than Section 7.3's anti-training prohibition, and it invites a fight.
- **Dribas has counterarguments, but they are not decisive.** DPA Section 2.3 says the SLA otherwise "remains unchanged," and the DPA's purpose is personal data (DPA Recital C). These are arguments, not certainty.

**Recommended fix:**
- Amend DPA Section 1.1 so the term is defined "for purposes of this Addendum only." Better still, rename it "**Customer Personal Data**" throughout the DPA.
- Add an express statement that nothing in the DPA narrows the SLA Section 1.4 definition or the SLA Section 7 protections.
- Ask Brikon in the meantime to confirm in writing that it has not used Dribas's non-personal data for any purpose other than serving Dribas.

---

### Priority 4 (Medium–High): The Exclusivity Covenant Is Far Broader Than the Agreed Term Sheet Scope

**Where:**
- SLA Section 2.5 (Exclusivity).
- SLA Schedule A Section A.7 (Pricing Basis).
- Term Sheet Section 5 (contrast).

**What the documents say:**
- **SLA covenant.** SLA Section 2.5 bars Dribas **and its Affiliates** from licensing, using or developing "any brewery management, inventory, **point-of-sale or distribution software** other than the Licensed Software, **anywhere in the world**," for the Term. It also requires BrewLedger to be the system of record for the functions it supports.
- **Agreed scope.** Term Sheet Section 5.1 limited exclusivity to **production-scheduling software at the Wilmington and Dover breweries only**. Section 5.2 expressly preserved Dribas's freedom to choose its own taproom POS, distributor and sales management, accounting and inventory systems, and bound Dribas only, not its Affiliates.
- **Integration clause.** SLA Section 15.7 supersedes term sheets, so Dribas cannot rely on the narrower scope. Brikon's December draft left Section 2.5 "[Reserved]", pending a separate circulation. The broad text appears to have entered late.

**Why it matters:**
- **Possible existing breach.** BrewLedger does not include a POS module (see Schedule A Section A.1). Dribas's Wilmington taproom presumably runs POS software today. If so, Dribas may *already* be in breach, which gives Brikon a counter-claim and leverage in the August Notice dispute.
- **Wider restrictions.** The covenant also limits:
  - distributor and sales platforms;
  - any future brewery, taproom or acquisition, through the Affiliate reach; and
  - any in-house development.
- **No termination or survival hook.** Section 2.5 is not listed in the SLA Section 12.6 survival clause, so it should end with the SLA. But it binds for the full Term, including renewals.
- **Brikon will cite the discount.** It will point to the approximately 20% discount in Section A.7 as consideration. That is the same discount the Term Sheet tied to the *narrow* covenant.

**Recommended fix:**
- Amend Section 2.5 to track Term Sheet Section 5. Exclusivity should be limited to **production-scheduling software at the Wilmington and Dover Sites**, bind Dribas only (not Affiliates), and permit parallel use during implementation and testing (Term Sheet Section 5.3).
- Seek an express acknowledgment that Dribas's existing POS, distribution and inventory tools do not breach Section 2.5, with a release of any past-breach claim.
- **Action item:** confirm with the client what non-BrewLedger systems Dribas and its Affiliates use today.

---

### Priority 5 (Medium): The DPA's New York Governing Law and Forum Splits Data-Related Disputes Away from Delaware

**Where:**
- DPA Section 12 (Sections 12.1 and 12.2).
- SLA Sections 15.1 and 15.6.

**What the documents say:**
- **SLA choice.** SLA Section 15.1 chooses **Delaware** law and the **exclusive** jurisdiction of the state or federal courts in **New Castle County, Delaware**. The Term Sheet (Section 13.1), the Side Letter (Section 9.5) and the Amendment (Section 9.4) all follow Delaware.
- **DPA choice.** DPA Section 12 provides that the DPA *and any claim "arising out of or relating to … the Processing of Customer Data"* is governed by **New York** law. Such claims must be brought exclusively in the courts of **New York County, New York**.
- **Precedence.** The DPA prevails under SLA Section 15.6, so the New York clause controls data-related claims.

**Why it matters:**
- **One incident, two forums.** A single event could be litigated in two courts under two bodies of law. Examples include a data breach, an outage that corrupts production or batch records, or Brikon's misuse of Dribas's data. This matters most for **data-related claims**, which are likely the most consequential claims Dribas could have against a hosted platform.
- **Dribas loses its home forum.** Dribas is a Delaware company dealing with a Wilmington-based vendor. It would lose its home forum and face added cost, inconsistent rulings and arguments over which clause governs.
- **The forum fight could follow the scope fight.** The scope of "Processing of Customer Data" also depends on the narrowed definition in Priority 3. That invites threshold litigation over where a claim belongs.

**Recommended fix:**
- Amend DPA Section 12 to apply Delaware law and the New Castle County forum. Alternatively, delete Sections 12.1 and 12.2 and cross-refer to SLA Sections 15.1 and 15.2, as the Side Letter and the Amendment already do.
- Add a clause stating that any dispute involving both the SLA and the DPA is resolved in a single proceeding under SLA Section 15.1.

---

## 3. Other Observations (No Action Required Now)

- **Prior draft.** Brikon's December 19, 2025 draft is expressly superseded and has no operative effect. It is useful only as negotiation history. It shows that the exclusivity clause (Section 2.5) and the precedence clause (Section 15.6) were left open and settled late, and that the original Section 11.3(a) carve-out referred expressly to "Licensor's obligations under Section 10.1."
- **Board consent.** The Board approved the SLA, the Side Letter and the DPA, and directed management to calendar the Side Letter notice period (Section 6.5(a)). We should ask whether that calendar existed and why the July 30 date was missed. This is mainly an internal and governance point.
- **DPA Section 14.1.** DPA liability is subject to SLA Section 11. Once the carve-out in Priority 2 is fixed, we should confirm that the DPA does not reintroduce a cap on Brikon's data-breach obligations beyond what SLA Section 11.3(b) already excludes.

---

## 4. Recommended Path Forward

1. **Immediately:**
   - Advise the client in writing to continue performing under the SLA and keep its legacy systems in parallel.
   - Confirm the facts behind the August Notice: delivery date and method, and Board authorization.
   - Inventory Dribas's and its Affiliates' non-BrewLedger software.
2. **Within two weeks:**
   - Invoke SLA Section 14.1 escalation (expressly permitted by Amendment Section 6.4).
   - Propose **Amendment No. 2** covering:
     - (a) resolution of the August Notice, either through a negotiated exit or a fresh termination window tied to the BIM retest dates;
     - (b) repointing SLA Section 11.3(a) to Section 10.2 and capping Dribas's Section 10.1 indemnity;
     - (c) limiting the DPA "Customer Data" definition to the Addendum;
     - (d) narrowing SLA Section 2.5 to the Term Sheet scope, with a release; and
     - (e) conforming DPA Section 12 to Delaware.
3. **In parallel:**
   - Track the BIM Remediation Plan retest dates to preserve the SLA Section 4.4(c) Module termination right.
   - Prepare a Section 12.2 breach notice as a fallback if negotiations stall.

I am happy to prepare a draft of Amendment No. 2 and a client advice letter on the August Notice.

# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** Associate
**Date:** November 24, 2026
**Re:** Dribas Brewing Company, LLC / Brikon Systems, Inc.: Review of BrewLedger License Documents, Prioritized Issues and Recommended Fixes

---

## I. Summary

We reviewed all seven documents in the folder:

1. Software License Agreement dated January 15, 2026 (the "SLA")
2. Side Letter dated January 15, 2026
3. Amendment No. 1 dated September 15, 2026
4. Term Sheet dated December 8, 2025
5. Data Processing Addendum dated January 15, 2026 (the "DPA")
6. Brikon's prior draft of December 19, 2025
7. Dribas's Board/Member Consent dated January 12, 2026

**How the documents rank.** SLA Section 15.6 sets the order of precedence:

1. signed amendments and side letters;
2. then the DPA;
3. then the SLA.

So **where the DPA conflicts with the SLA, the DPA prevails.** That rule is central to two of the issues below. Under SLA Section 15.7 the Term Sheet and the prior draft are superseded and have no contractual effect. They are still useful evidence of what the parties agreed.

**Bottom line for the client.**

1. Dribas's August 14, 2026 termination notice was most likely sent after the Side Letter window closed. Dribas should not treat the SLA as terminated.
2. The DPA moves data-related disputes to New York law and New York courts.
3. The DPA's narrow definition of "Customer Data" may strip contractual protection from Dribas's recipes and production data.
4. The exclusivity covenant is far broader than the deal the parties agreed.

## II. Issues in Priority Order

### 1. HIGH / MOST URGENT: The Side Letter termination notice appears untimely

**Where:**
- Side Letter Section 2 (Sections 2.1 and 2.2)
- Amendment No. 1, Recitals B and C and Sections 5.7 and 6

**Issue.**
- Side Letter Section 2.1 required the Brewhouse Integration Module (BIM) to be Accepted at both Sites by the **Acceptance Deadline of June 30, 2026**.
- Section 2.2 gives Dribas a fee-free right to terminate the whole SLA if that does not happen. The Termination Notice must be "delivered no later than thirty (30) days after the Acceptance Deadline," which is **July 30, 2026**.
- Amendment Recital B confirms the BIM was not Accepted at either Site by the deadline, so the right was triggered.
- Recital C records that Dribas delivered the August Notice on **August 14, 2026**. That is 15 days after the window closed. The notice named a termination date of November 12, 2026.
- Brikon disputed the notice by letter dated August 28, 2026. Amendment Section 6 records that the dispute is unresolved and that both sides reserve all rights.

**Why it matters.**
- On the face of the documents, the notice was untimely and is likely ineffective to exercise the Termination Right.
- Nothing in the Side Letter extends the window:
  - Section 6.3 says Brikon's delay notices do not affect the Acceptance Deadline or the Termination Right.
  - Section 9.3 and SLA Section 15.8 require any waiver or amendment to be in a signed writing.
  - SLA Section 15.8 also provides that failure or delay in exercising a right is not a waiver. That protects reserved rights, but it does not revive a lapsed exercise period.
- The November 12, 2026 date in the notice has now passed. If Dribas acts as though the SLA has ended, it could itself be in breach and give Brikon a Section 12.2 termination or damages claim. Examples would be:
  - stopping payment of the annual subscription Fees;
  - refusing performance; or
  - migrating off the platform.
- Losing the Side Letter right also means losing the full implementation fee refund in Side Letter Section 3.1(b).
- Two governance points under the Board Consent:
  - Section 9.3(a) requires prior Board approval of any termination notice, subject to a CEO emergency exception. We should confirm the August Notice was properly authorized.
  - Section 6.5 required the project manager and counsel to calendar this notice period. Whether that was done is relevant internally.

**Recommended fix / next steps.**
1. Advise the client in writing to keep performing and paying undisputed Fees under SLA Section 14.3 and Amendment Section 6.3. Dribas should not decommission systems on the assumption the SLA has terminated. Side Letter Section 4.6 and Amendment Section 5.6 preserve its right to run legacy systems in parallel.
2. Rely on the reservation of rights in Amendment Section 6.2 and the "without prejudice" language in Section 5.7. Avoid any statement that concedes the lapse.
3. Pursue a negotiated resolution. Options include a signed waiver or extension of the Section 2.2 window, or a fresh, dated termination right tied to the BIM Remediation Plan dates in Amendment Section 5.1(d). Escalation under SLA Section 14.1 is available now (Amendment Section 6.4).
4. Preserve alternative exit routes that do not depend on the Side Letter window:
   - **SLA Section 4.4(c):** Module-level termination and refund if the BIM fails after the second retest.
   - **SLA Section 9.3:** termination for warranty failure.
   - **SLA Section 12.2:** termination for material breach after a 30-day cure period. Possible grounds are the missed Acceptance Deadline and any failure to deliver the Side Letter Section 6.3 delay notices.
   - **SLA Section 5.5:** chronic availability failure, if the facts support it.

   Document the BIM latency and data-loss failures now.
5. Confirm Board authorization under Board Consent Section 9.3 before sending any further notice.

### 2. HIGH: DPA's "Customer Data" definition overrides the SLA and may leave recipes and production data unprotected

**Where:**
- DPA Section 1.1
- SLA Sections 1.4, 7.3 and 15.6

**Issue.**
- **SLA Section 1.4** defines "Customer Data" broadly: "all data Licensee submits, including recipes, formulations, production records and distributor sales data," plus derived outputs.
- **SLA Section 7.3** bars Brikon from using Customer Data except to provide the services. In particular, Brikon may not use it to "develop, train, benchmark or improve products or services for any other person."
- **DPA Section 1.1** defines the same capitalized term as only "Personal Data that Licensor Processes on behalf of Licensee." The definition is not limited to the DPA itself.
- Because the DPA outranks the SLA under Section 15.6, Brikon can argue that the narrow definition controls throughout.

**Why it matters.**
- If that argument succeeds, the Section 7.3 use restriction protects only personal data. The same is true of these other provisions:
  - ownership (Section 7.1);
  - security (Section 7.4);
  - return and deletion (Section 7.8);
  - the uncapped liability exception for breach of Sections 7.3 and 7.4 (Section 11.3(b)).
- Dribas's recipes, formulations and production records would then fall outside these protections. The Board Consent (Section 8.2) identifies those records as "among its most valuable trade secrets."
- Brikon could then use that data to train or benchmark across other brewery customers. The confidentiality provisions in SLA Section 8 give some fallback protection, but they are weaker and fact-dependent.
- The Term Sheet (Section 8.1) confirms the broad definition was the agreed deal.

**Recommended fix.**
1. Amend the DPA so that its definition applies only "for purposes of this Addendum," or replace it with a distinct term such as "Customer Personal Data."
2. Add an express statement that nothing in the DPA narrows the SLA's definition of Customer Data or Brikon's obligations under SLA Section 7.
3. This is a low-cost clarification that Brikon should find hard to resist, since it matches the Term Sheet. Raise it in the same negotiation as Issue 1.

### 3. HIGH / MEDIUM: DPA's New York law and forum clause splits data disputes away from Delaware

**Where:**
- DPA Section 12 (Sections 12.1 and 12.2)
- SLA Sections 15.1 and 15.6

**Issue.**
- **SLA Section 15.1** chooses Delaware law and the exclusive jurisdiction of the state or federal courts in New Castle County, Delaware. The Term Sheet (Section 13.1), the Side Letter (Section 9.5) and the Amendment (Section 9.4) all follow this choice.
- **DPA Section 12** provides that the DPA and "any claim... arising out of or relating to... the Processing of Customer Data" are governed by **New York law**. Such claims must be brought exclusively in the courts of **New York County, New York**.
- Because the DPA prevails under SLA Section 15.6, the New York clause controls data-related claims.

**Why it matters.**
- A single incident could have to be litigated in two forums under two bodies of law. Examples include:
  - a data breach;
  - an outage that corrupts batch or compliance records;
  - misuse of production data.

  The contract claims would go to Delaware and the data-related claims to New York.
- This raises costs and risks inconsistent results. It also gives Brikon a forum argument on exactly the claims most likely to matter to a Delaware brewer.
- "Processing of Customer Data" is broad. Its reach also depends on how Issue 2 is resolved.
- Every party, every Site and the relevant regulators are in Delaware. There is no apparent business reason for New York.

**Recommended fix.**
1. Amend DPA Section 12 to apply SLA Section 15.1, meaning Delaware law and the New Castle County courts, to all disputes under the DPA.
2. At a minimum, add that any claim arising from a single set of facts under both documents may be brought in the SLA forum.
3. Bundle this with the Issue 2 amendment.

### 4. MEDIUM: Exclusivity covenant is far broader than the Term Sheet deal

**Where:**
- SLA Section 2.5 and Schedule A, Section A.7
- Compare Term Sheet Section 5

**Issue.**
- **SLA Section 2.5** bars Dribas and its Affiliates from licensing, using or developing "any brewery management, inventory, point-of-sale or distribution software other than the Licensed Software, anywhere in the world," for the full Term.
- **Term Sheet Section 5.1** limits exclusivity to **production-scheduling software at the Wilmington and Dover breweries only**.
- **Term Sheet Section 5.2** expressly preserves Dribas's freedom to choose its own taproom point-of-sale, distributor and sales management, accounting and inventory systems. It also says the covenant binds Dribas only, not its Affiliates.
- Brikon's December 19 draft left Section 2.5 "[Reserved]" pending separate circulation. The broad language therefore appears to have come in late.

**Why it matters.**
- Read literally, Dribas is already in technical breach if its Wilmington taproom runs any third-party point-of-sale system. BrewLedger does not appear to offer point-of-sale functionality.
- The same applies to any separate distributor or accounting-adjacent inventory tool Dribas uses.
- The covenant would also restrict any future brewery, any Affiliate, and any acquisition.
- The covenant runs for the full Term, including auto-renewals under Section 12.1. If Issue 1 cannot be resolved, Dribas is locked in through at least January 2029.
- The SLA integration clause (Section 15.7) expressly supersedes the Term Sheet. Dribas therefore cannot rely on the narrower agreed scope, other than as evidence in a reformation or mutual-mistake argument.

**Recommended fix.**
1. Amend Section 2.5 to match Term Sheet Section 5:
   - production-scheduling software only;
   - Wilmington and Dover Sites only;
   - Dribas only, not Affiliates;
   - parallel use permitted during implementation;
   - automatic end on termination or expiry.
2. Ask Brikon to confirm in writing, in the meantime, that it will not assert breach for Dribas's existing point-of-sale, distribution or inventory tools.
3. Use the Term Sheet and the prior draft as negotiating leverage. Brikon's 20% discount (Schedule A, Section A.7) was priced against the narrow covenant.

## III. Distractor Documents
